title: Prominent U.S. archbishop compares planned livestream of firing squad execution to terrorist practices
summary: Catholics serving in the U.S. army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood ‌shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S.…

image.caption: U.S. Military Services Archbishop Timothy Broglio, seen here in 2025, has raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to ​broadcast the execution of a former U.S. army officer who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. (Stephanie Scarbrough/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Catholics serving in the U.S. army should not participate in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood ‌shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to livestream in December, a prominent U.S. archbishop said on Monday.
Timothy Broglio urged Catholic members assigned to the firing squad to request religious exemption

In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the U.S. armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to ​broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort ​Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.

Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan's victims, and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the U.S. ​wanted to "imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically ⁠killing our adversaries."
"I oblige any Catholics ⁠assigned to the firing squad to request to be ‌excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church," Broglio said.
U.S. army regulations do allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations, and the army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad.
The Pentagon says Nidal Hasan will be executed by firing squad in a livestreamed broadcast in December. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Handout/Reuters)

U.S. War Secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth announced plans to livestream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and international observers. U.S. President Donald Trump approved Hasan's execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the ‌livestreaming to proceed.

The event would be extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the U.S. military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been ​shot by police during his arrest.

The U.S. plans to livestream an execution. Here's how that compares to global practice

blocks.text: Hegseth said last week he wants U.S. soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and ⁠location of Hasan's shooting spree. Hegseth has argued that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent.

Broglio ⁠questioned whether the effect of a livestreamed execution on young viewers had been considered. He said the U.S. military ⁠had ⁠a good reputation and asked if there ​was "really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of ​a man in a wheelchair to ⁠the whole world."

Broglio's statement was issued shortly after he met on Monday in Rome with Pope Leo, who has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war. Leo on Saturday condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically.
U.S. Vice-President JD Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get livestreamed, he would ⁠not watch it.
